research_text:
## Research brief

### Sources reviewed

* Oracle Java SE 25 API: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))  
* Oracle Java SE 25 API: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))  
* Oracle Java SE 25 API: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))  
* Oracle Java SE 8 API: `https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))  
* Supplied rule source: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))  

## 1. Governed API and the reported “no preparation” finding

`java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec` is a transparent key-specification class representing an **ASN.1 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` encoding of a public key**. The documented structure includes an `AlgorithmIdentifier` and a `subjectPublicKey` bit string. Its format name is `"X.509"`. This is a public-key encoding specification; the API documentation does not describe it as an X.509 certificate object or certificate-path representation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

The Java API does **not** document an event named “preparation,” nor a `preparedKeyMaterial` value or validation state. The applicable rule source instead declares a rule-local requirement named `preparedKeyMaterial[encodedKey]` for the constructor event. Therefore, the documented value to which this particular rule refers is the constructor’s `byte[] encodedKey` argument, and the rule-local event is construction using `X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey)`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

The rule source gives no definition of what makes `encodedKey` “prepared,” no producer of that predicate, and no runtime test for it. Consequently, the source does **not** support concluding that the bytes are malformed, that a particular Java API validation failed, or that the predicate is false at runtime. The meaning of a detector message saying that preparation “was observed” is unresolved from this rule source alone.

## 2. Documented correct/safe usage and documented remediation

### Documented API semantics

Oracle documents the one-argument constructor as accepting a key that is **assumed to be encoded according to the X.509 standard**. It copies the supplied byte array, protecting the specification object from later mutation of the caller’s array; it throws `NullPointerException` when the array is `null`. `getEncoded()` returns an X.509 encoding in a new array on each invocation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

The two-argument constructor accepts the same encoded public-key material plus an algorithm name. Oracle states that this overload is useful where later consumers of the specification might not know the key algorithm; it rejects `null` values and an empty algorithm string. The documentation points to the Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification for standard asymmetric-key algorithm names. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

The documented conversion API is `KeyFactory`: it converts between opaque `Key` objects and transparent `KeySpec` representations. `KeyFactory.generatePublic(KeySpec)` generates a `PublicKey` from the supplied key specification and throws `InvalidKeySpecException` if the specification is inappropriate for that key factory. Oracle’s example constructs an `X509EncodedKeySpec` from an encoded public key and passes it to a matching `KeyFactory`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

### Remediation stated by official sources

The reviewed Oracle API sources do **not** provide a remediation instruction for a condition called `preparedKeyMaterial`, nor do they define a preparation operation that must precede construction. They document the expected representation—an X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` public-key encoding—and the use of `KeyFactory` to convert an appropriate specification to a public key. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

Accordingly, there is **no official, documented remediation for this specific rule predicate** in the reviewed Java API documentation. Any claim that a particular normalization, parser, validation routine, provenance check, or other preprocessing step satisfies `preparedKeyMaterial` would require documentation outside this rule file; that evidence was not present in the supplied rule source.

## 3. Compatibility, persisted/wire formats, version support, and migration

### Persisted and wire-format semantics

The Java `Key` API documents an encoded key as an **external encoded form** used when a standard representation is needed outside the JVM, including transmission to another party. It identifies X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` as the ASN.1 data format for public keys and associates that format with the name `"X.509"`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

`X509EncodedKeySpec` specifically represents that public-key encoding, and `getEncoded()` is documented to return the X.509 encoding. Thus, changing away from this specification class or passing material in a different representation changes the documented representation contract. The reviewed documentation does not provide a general byte-for-byte persistence guarantee, a wire-protocol migration procedure, or a conversion mapping between this format and unrelated containers or certificate encodings. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

### Platform-version support

* The class and its one-argument constructor, `X509EncodedKeySpec(byte[] encodedKey)`, are documented as present since Java 1.2. Oracle’s Java SE 8 documentation shows that constructor and the same X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` purpose. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))  
* The overload `X509EncodedKeySpec(byte[] encodedKey, String algorithm)` is documented as available since Java 9. Therefore, code using that overload has a Java 9-or-later platform requirement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))  

### Documented migration path

No reviewed official source provides a migration path specifically for changing construction or “preparing” the `encodedKey` value. The `KeyFactory` API documents conversion between compatible key specifications and keys, but does not specify a migration procedure for this Crypto-API-Rules predicate or for persisted application formats. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

**Source limitation:** provider support and acceptance of a particular `KeySpec` remain tied to the selected `KeyFactory`; the API documents `InvalidKeySpecException` where the supplied specification is inappropriate. The sources reviewed do not establish compatibility for any particular provider, key algorithm, stored data population, or protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

## 4. Exact matching rule in `X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl`

The supplied rule’s governing type is explicitly the fully qualified Java type:

```text
SPEC java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec
```

Its declared object and event clauses are:

```text
OBJECTS
    byte[] encodedKey;

EVENTS
    c1: X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey);
    Con := c1;
```

The rule source is: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

### What it matches

* **Receiver/governed type:** `java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec`, as specified by the `SPEC` clause. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))  
* **Method names:** the source declares **no ordinary method-call events**. It declares the constructor-like event `X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey)`. Because this is construction, there is no instance receiver variable stated in the rule. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))  
* **Parameter list:** yes. The sole declared event has exactly one named argument, `encodedKey`; the `OBJECTS` section declares that argument as `byte[]`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))  
* **Event alias:** `Con` is assigned as an alias for `c1`, and the `ORDER` section requires `Con`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))  

### Condition evaluated after the matching event

The source’s complete requirement clause is:

```text
REQUIRES
    preparedKeyMaterial[encodedKey];
```

It also declares the following postcondition:

```text
ENSURES
    speccedKey[this, _] after Con;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

There is no `CONSTRAINTS` section and no runtime value predicate in this source file. In particular, the source does not state a condition based on algorithm, key size, certificate-chain status, key provenance, or later use. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

### Can this rule match a method merely because it shares the API’s name?

**According to the rule text itself, no.** It scopes the specification to `java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec` and declares only the one-argument constructor-shaped event `X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey)`; it does not declare an event for a method merely sharing that name. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

**Limitation:** the `.crysl` file does not document the analyzer’s type-resolution, overload-resolution, or call-graph behavior. Therefore, this source supports the rule-text conclusion above, but it cannot establish how any particular detector implementation handles unresolved types, namesakes, reflection, or incomplete dependencies.
